explain.say: Imagine a super fast chef who reads one line of a recipe, works out what it means, does it, then moves to the next line, over and over. That chef is the CPU, the brain chip of a computer. Look at the circle on the board: it is the CPU's never ending loop.

faq.q: What does fetch mean in a CPU?
faq.a: Fetch is the first step: the CPU copies the next instruction from memory, using the program counter to know where it is, into the processor.
asks: Where does the CPU get instructions from?

faq.a: Decode is the step where the control unit works out what the fetched instruction means, such as add, compare or jump, and gets ready to do it.
asks: What does the control unit do?

faq.a: Execute is the step where the CPU carries out the instruction, for example the arithmetic logic unit adds two numbers, and the result is stored.
The CPU, central processing unit, follows a program one instruction at a time, fetching, decoding and executing each one. It does all the calculations and decisions in a computer.
asks: Why is the CPU called the brain of the computer?

faq.a: Gigahertz means billions of ticks per second, so a 3 GHz CPU has a clock that ticks 3 billion times a second. Modern CPUs also have several cores, each running its own cycle.

facts: One gigahertz is one billion cycles per second.
The fetch-decode-execute cycle comes from the design described by John von Neumann in 1945, where programs and data share the same memory.

quiz.say: Put the CPU steps in order. What comes straight after fetch?
quiz.why: The CPU must work out what the instruction means before it can do it: fetch, decode, execute.

wrong.1: Execute comes after decode, once the CPU knows what to do.
wrong.2: The cycle never stops while the computer is on.

quiz.say: Where does the CPU fetch its instructions from?
quiz.why: Programs are loaded into memory, and the CPU fetches each instruction from there.

wrong.2: The keyboard gives input, but programs wait in memory.
